title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
lead: An imminent steel strike leads President Truman to seize the mills, and their owners obtain an injunction while the Justices disagree over how Congress constrained emergency power.

actors.name: President Harry Truman
actors.role: Ordered federal possession and operation of steel mills.

actors.name: Charles Sawyer
actors.role: Secretary of Commerce who carried out the seizure.

actors.name: Steel companies
actors.role: Owners challenging possession and operation of their businesses.

actors.name: United Steelworkers
actors.role: Union negotiating new agreements and preparing an industry-wide strike.

proceedings: The district court issued a preliminary injunction on April 30, 1952; the D.C. Circuit stayed it.
The Supreme Court granted review of the companies’ petition and Sawyer’s cross-petition.
The Supreme Court affirmed the district court’s judgment, sustaining the preliminary injunction, 6–3.
limits: Jackson’s three categories and the other separate rationales must remain attributed. The Court did not decide the legality of the Korean military commitment or all future emergency seizures.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Negotiations fail during the Korean conflict
sections.cue: What had happened before the President took the mills?
paragraphs: The steel companies and the United Steelworkers negotiated replacement collective bargaining agreements during the Korean conflict. Their agreements expired December 31, 1951. A threatened strike and failed federal mediation led President Harry Truman to refer the dispute to the Wage Stabilization Board on December 22. The Board proposed terms, but no settlement followed. The union set an industry-wide strike for 12:01 a.m. on April 9, 1952.

Truman considered uninterrupted steel indispensable to weapons, defense materials, and national security. On April 8, shortly before the strike, Executive Order 10340 directed Secretary of Commerce Charles Sawyer to take possession of most steel mills and operate them. Sawyer immediately appointed the company presidents operating managers for the United States. They complied under protest.

The order authorized possession, operation, employment terms, regulations, and delegated authority. Existing management, payments, and obligations continued unless Sawyer directed otherwise; plants could return when possession was unnecessary and continued operation assured. Its basis was an aggregate claim of constitutional and statutory power, not compliance with a particular seizure statute. Truman reported to Congress on April 9 and April 21. Congress had not acted on those reports when the case was decided, but earlier procurement and labor-emergency legislation already occupied the field.

sections.title: The companies secure a preliminary injunction
sections.cue: Why could the courts decide legality before a damages action or final injunction?
paragraphs: The companies sued Sawyer for declarations of invalidity and preliminary and permanent injunctions. They argued that seizure made law entrusted to Congress. The Government invoked inherent authority, historic practice, the executive power, the Take Care Clause, and military command to prevent catastrophe. It separately argued that compensation was available and irreparable harm absent.

The district court rejected those defenses and issued a preliminary injunction on April 30. The D.C. Circuit stayed it that day. The Supreme Court granted review May 3 on the companies’ petition and Sawyer’s cross-petition, then heard argument May 12–13. The legality issue was ripe at that preliminary stage: precedent left uncertain whether the Court of Claims could compensate an unlawful official taking, and operating ongoing businesses caused present and future injuries difficult or impossible to reduce to money.

Justice Black wrote the Court’s opinion. Frankfurter, Douglas, Jackson, and Burton joined it and wrote separately; Clark concurred only in the judgment. Chief Justice Vinson dissented with Reed and Minton. This alignment produced five distinct concurrences, not a single shared explanation supplementing Black.

sections.title: Black finds no source for this seizure
sections.cue: How did the order depart from executing laws Congress had made?
paragraphs: Black required authority from Congress or the Constitution. No statute expressly or fairly impliedly authorized this taking. The Selective Service Act and Defense Production Act permitted acquisition under conditions the Government conceded it had not met. Calling the statutory process cumbersome did not dispense with it. In Taft-Hartley Congress rejected general emergency plant-seizure authority and chose mediation, inquiry, reporting, and temporary strike injunctions while ultimately preserving a right to strike.

Military command did not authorize domestic seizure to avert production losses in a labor dispute. Decisions about military commanders in a theater of operations did not control. The Take Care duty presupposed law to execute; it did not supply legislative power. Truman’s order prescribed its own policy and the rules to implement it. Congress could authorize takings and regulate labor, wages, and dispute settlement, but those powers were not subject to presidential control. Earlier executive seizures could not transfer Congress’s lawmaking function.

sections.title: Frankfurter and Douglas reach the same result by distinct routes
sections.cue: What did history and appropriations add to their accounts?
paragraphs: Frankfurter emphasized flexibility in separation of powers while finding an affirmative congressional policy against general seizure. Repeated enactments imposed limits on duration, emergencies, refusal of government orders, responsible agencies, and compensation. Taft-Hartley reserved fresh seizure authority for congressional action in a particular emergency. Defense Production Act mediation and Wage Stabilization Board arrangements did not turn voluntary settlement machinery into coercive possession. Equity could not disregard Congress’s balancing of interests.

For Frankfurter, systematic, unbroken, previously unquestioned practice known to Congress might supply constitutional gloss. Midwest Oil’s established land withdrawals differed from these seizures. Wilson’s actions invoked statutes; many Roosevelt actions were statutory or followed declared war. Three potentially comparable 1941 seizures were too isolated, and he did not decide their validity. His appendices compare eighteen enactments or amendments and trace wartime, labor, and nonlabor seizures with source qualifications and unknowns. They support his historical reasoning, not extra holdings. He reserved cases with no relevant legislation and genuinely limited seizures expiring without approval. Emergency assertions could not automatically insulate executive action from review; distributed power deliberately entails friction.

Douglas distinguished a grave occasion for action from a source of power. Even temporary industry seizure was a taking requiring compensation, and Congress’s control of revenue and payment meant Congress must authorize or ratify condemnation. Military command gave no general civilian authority. Leadership, recommendations, and persuasion remained available. Allowing seizure to raise wages would equally authorize a later President to use it against labor; structural change could not depend on today’s convenience.

sections.title: Jackson places the seizure at the lowest level of presidential authority
sections.cue: Why was this not simply congressional silence?
paragraphs: Jackson described separated but interdependent institutions rather than judging permanent power by the current President or policy. When Congress expressly or impliedly authorizes action, presidential authority includes his own powers plus what Congress may delegate and receives the strongest presumption. With neither grant nor denial, independent and possibly concurrent authority forms a zone of uncertain allocation: inertia may enable action in practice, but silence is not invariably permission. Against Congress’s expressed or implied will, presidential power is lowest; sustaining exclusive executive control requires excluding Congress from the subject.

This seizure fell in the third situation. The conceded absence of statutory authority excluded the first. Government procurement orders, condemnation, and labor-emergency procedures supplied inconsistent congressional policies, excluding an open field for the second. Their prerequisites had not been used. Upholding seizure would make strike-bound industry an exclusive presidential domain beyond Congress, which Jackson rejected. His discussion distinguished Curtiss-Wright’s delegated authority from unilateral action.

Neither a bulk reading of executive power nor military command supplied that exclusivity. Sending troops abroad did not enlarge domestic control; Jackson expressly reserved the legality of the Korean enterprise. Congress controlled raising, supporting, and supplying forces and restricted domestic military use. Lawful outward command merited latitude, but a lawful internal labor dispute was different. The Take Care duty reached only as far as law allowed.

Jackson rejected undefined emergency authority and treated even his own earlier executive advocacy as no binding precedent. His discussion distinguished North American Aviation’s contracts, property, consent, and insurrection-like circumstances; comparisons with foreign emergency regimes favored independent controls. Congress could activate substantial emergency powers, while presidential influence, communication, and party leadership already supplied practical strength. Congress had to act timely to preserve its responsibilities.

sections.title: Burton and Clark insist on the statutory routes; Vinson reads those routes differently
sections.cue: How did the Justices differ about emergency authority and congressional policy?
paragraphs: Burton found that Congress had anticipated this kind of emergency and retained further seizure authorization. Failed mediation did not become seizure power merely because it produced delay comparable to Taft-Hartley. Neither condemnation nor compulsory defense orders had been tried. He reserved catastrophic cases such as imminent invasion, threatened attack, or total-war command.

Clark affirmatively accepted extensive independent emergency authority where Congress had supplied no controlling procedure, but Little v. Barreme showed that statutory directions displace a different executive method. Here Congress allowed mediation and ordinary condemnation, an eighty-day Taft-Hartley injunction and report, and seizure after refusal or failure of properly placed defense orders. Ninety-nine days of mediation did not convert one route into another. The Government had not explained why prompt compulsory orders were unavailable; Clark cited rapid historical seizures after such orders and noted that an order need not occupy all a plant’s capacity.

Vinson’s dissent emphasized uncontested affidavits about weapons, ammunition, defense facilities, scarce inventories, and shutdown consequences. Assuming judicial review and, without deciding, review of the emergency finding, he considered the crisis proved. He saw seizure as preserving Congress’s defense procurement and anti-inflation programs: shutdown defeated procurement, while the industry’s price demand threatened stabilization. Temporary possession, prompt reports, willingness to follow Congress’s response, and compensation accompanied that preservation.

The dissent’s historical examples included neutrality, treaties, Lincoln, Neagle, Debs, Midwest Oil, and industrial seizures. It disputed the majority’s statutory history, regarded Taft-Hartley as a discretionary peacetime route alongside later defense machinery, and emphasized Congress’s retention of Board dispute functions and mediation exceeding eighty days. It did not claim power to disregard an express prohibition or defy Congress indefinitely; it construed Congress’s policy differently and would have reversed the injunction.

sources.pinpoint: Burton concurrence 655–660; Clark concurrence 660–667; Vinson dissent 667–710

sections.title: The injunction survives
sections.cue: Which judgment did the Supreme Court affirm?
paragraphs: On June 2, 1952, the Court affirmed the district court’s judgment, sustaining its preliminary injunction by six votes to three. It did not affirm the appellate stay. The seizure was unauthorized and could be restrained at this stage.

The assigned editorial account emphasizes Jackson’s framework and Frankfurter’s gloss but does not reproduce all writings. Its grouping of Burton and Clark must not erase Burton’s reservation of catastrophic circumstances versus Clark’s affirmative acceptance of independent authority absent controlling legislation. The dissent relied on combined executive responsibilities and preservation of Congress’s programs, not military command alone. None of these separate formulations transforms silence into automatic permission, every rejected bill into a constitutional prohibition, or each Justice’s view into the Court’s holding.
